title: What does 925 sterling silver mean? A simple guide
description: 925 sterling silver means 92.5% pure silver mixed with other metals for strength. Learn what the stamp tells you, what it doesn't, and what to check first.
intro: 925 sterling silver is an alloy made of 92.5% pure silver and 7.5% other metals, most often copper. The number 925 simply means 925 parts silver out of every 1,000. It is real silver, just made a little tougher so it can survive being worn as jewellery.

sections.heading: The number, decoded
paragraphs: Jewellers describe silver purity in parts per thousand. Fine silver, the purest form you will usually see, is marked 999, meaning 99.9% silver. Sterling silver is marked 925, meaning 92.5% silver. You may also hear Indian shopkeepers call it '92.5 silver' or 'ninety-two-and-a-half', which is the same thing said as a percentage.

The remaining 7.5% is there on purpose. It is not a cheat or a filler. Copper is the traditional partner because it makes the metal harder without changing its colour much. Some makers use small amounts of zinc or other metals in the mix, which is why two sterling pieces can feel or tarnish slightly differently.

sections.heading: Why jewellery is not made from pure silver
paragraphs: Pure silver is beautiful but soft. A thin chain or a pendant bail made from 999 silver would bend, stretch and scratch quickly with daily wear. Stone settings would loosen because the metal cannot hold a claw firmly for long.

Adding that 7.5% of copper gives sterling enough strength to hold a cubic zirconia in place, keep a clasp working and survive being pulled over your head every morning. That is why 999 silver is usually sold as coins, bars and utensils, while most wearable silver jewellery is 925.

sections.heading: Where to find the 925 mark on a piece
paragraphs: On pendants, look on the back of the pendant or on the bail, the small loop the chain passes through. On chains, the mark is usually on the clasp or on a tiny tag near it. Rings carry it inside the band. The stamp may read '925', 'S925', 'Sterling' or 'Ster', and it is often so small that you need your phone camera zoomed in to read it.

Some pieces also carry a hallmark from a testing centre along with the purity number. Rules around silver hallmarking can change, so the practical advice is simple: look for a stamp or hallmark, and if you cannot find one, ask the seller directly what the purity is and how they can show it.

sections.heading: What the 925 stamp does not tell you
paragraphs: A stamp tells you about the metal, and nothing else. It is worth knowing its limits before you treat it as proof of quality.
list: It does not tell you about plating. Many 925 pieces are coated in rhodium for a brighter white look, or in gold for a yellow finish. The base is still sterling.
It does not describe the stones. A CZ, a natural gemstone and glass can all sit in a 925 setting.
It does not speak for craftsmanship. Solder joints, clasp quality and how well stones are set vary from maker to maker.
It can be faked. A stamp is just an impression in metal, so buy from sellers who answer questions clearly and offer returns.

sections.heading: How 925 silver behaves once you own it
paragraphs: Because sterling contains copper and silver, it reacts with sulphur compounds in the air and slowly darkens. This is called tarnish, and it is a sign of real silver rather than a defect. A soft polishing cloth or a mild wash brings back the shine, and with sensible storage, tarnish builds up slowly.

Sterling is also durable in the long run. Unlike plated imitation jewellery, there is no thin coating to wear through and reveal a different metal underneath, unless the piece was gold or rhodium plated to begin with. Scratches can be buffed out by a jeweller, and a well-made pendant can last for many years.

sections.heading: A quick checklist before you buy 925 silver
paragraphs: If you are buying online, the product page should state the metal clearly. Varaha's [925 sterling silver pendants](/silver), for example, list the metal, plating and stone type on each listing. Wherever you shop, run through these points:
list: Is the metal stated as 925 or sterling, not just 'silver colour' or 'silver tone'?
Is any plating mentioned, and in what colour?
What are the stones, and are they set with claws or glued in?
Does the chain come with the pendant, and is the chain also 925?
Is there a return window if the piece arrives different from the description?

faq.a: Yes. It is 92.5% pure silver. The small share of other metals makes it strong enough to wear, which is why it is the standard for silver jewellery.

faq.q: Is 92.5 silver the same as 925 silver?
faq.a: Yes. 92.5 is the percentage and 925 is the parts-per-thousand figure. Both describe sterling silver.
It can darken over time as it reacts with sulphur in the air. This tarnish is surface-level and can be cleaned with a polishing cloth or a gentle wash.

faq.q: Is 925 silver better than 999 silver for jewellery?
faq.a: For everyday jewellery, usually yes. 999 is purer but much softer, so it bends and scratches easily. 925 holds its shape and stones better.
